objectives: Explain what LayerNorm normalizes and why

slides.title: Part 1 — Why normalization exists
slides.body: Stack two dozen blocks naively and activations drift until training diverges. Normalization is the unglamorous fix that makes depth possible at all.

slides.title: The problem: activation drift compounds with depth
slides.body: Each sublayer adds its output into the residual stream. Without re-standardization, the activation scale performs a random walk that *compounds* across layers: by layer 20 some features sit at $10^3$, others at $10^{-3}$. This phenomenon — **internal covariate shift** — was named and studied by **Sergey Ioffe** and **Christian Szegedy** in their landmark paper *"Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift"* (ICML 2015). Their diagnosis: as parameters update during training, the distribution of each layer's inputs shifts, forcing subsequent layers to constantly re-adapt. Saturating nonlinearities (and softmax inside attention) then operate in flat regions where gradients vanish; the loss becomes hypersensitive to initialization and learning rate. We need to re-fix the scale **at every layer**, cheaply, without destroying the information.

slides.title: What LayerNorm does
slides.body:
**LayerNorm** was introduced by **Jimmy Lei Ba**, **Jamie Ryan Kiros**, and **Geoffrey Hinton** in *"Layer Normalization"* (arXiv 2016). For each token vector $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ *independently*, compute the mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ **across that token's $d$ features**, then $\text{LN}(x)=\gamma\odot\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}}+\beta$. The normalize step pins the distribution (mean 0, var 1) so scale can't drift; the learned per-feature $\gamma,\beta$ let the layer re-express *whatever* scale/shift it actually needs, so normalization costs no representational power. $\epsilon$ (e.g. $10^{-5}$) prevents divide-by-zero for low-variance tokens.

Critically, LayerNorm operates **per token, over the feature dimension** — it has no dependence on other tokens or other examples in the batch. This is what makes it the right normalization for sequence models: a sentence of 5 tokens and a sentence of 500 tokens are treated identically, and batch size of 1 at inference is handled without any special logic.

slides.title: LayerNorm vs BatchNorm — the decisive difference
slides.body:
**Batch Normalization** (Ioffe and Szegedy, ICML 2015) normalizes each *feature across the batch*, so its statistics depend on batch size and on the *other examples* in the batch. For sequences that's fatal: variable lengths, tiny inference batches (batch=1 in generation), and train/inference statistic mismatch all break it. **LayerNorm** (Ba, Kiros, and Hinton, 2016) normalizes **per token across features** — completely independent of batch size and of other examples; identical behavior at batch 1 or 4096, train or serve. That independence — not a marginal accuracy delta — is *why* transformers use LayerNorm and not BatchNorm.

This distinction matters enormously in practice: **GPT** (Radford et al., OpenAI 2018), **BERT** (Devlin et al., Google 2019), and all subsequent large language models including **GPT-2**, **GPT-3**, and **LLaMA** use LayerNorm throughout. BatchNorm remains dominant in vision models (ResNets, etc.) where batch statistics are stable and sequences don't vary in length, but it is essentially absent from production transformer LLMs.

question.question: For an input of shape [batch, seq_len, d_model], which axis does layer norm reduce over?
question.explanation: For each (batch, seq position), LN computes mean/std across the d_model feature axis. That batch- and length-independence is exactly why it behaves identically at training and inference — the whole reason it replaced batch norm in transformers.

question.question: A model trained with batch norm is served at batch_size = 1 in training mode. What breaks?
options: Per-batch stats become meaningless (the 'mean' is the single input); only running-average eval mode is correct — forgetting to switch silently corrupts outputs
Nothing — batch norm is batch-size independent
Activations always explode regardless of mode
question.explanation: Batch norm has two stat sources: per-batch (train) and running averages (eval). At batch_size = 1 the per-batch 'statistics' are degenerate. `model.eval()` switches to running averages; forgetting it is a classic deployment bug. Layer norm sidesteps it entirely.

question.question: Blow the input scale up to 100× — LayerNorm output std should stay ≈ 1 (target ≤ 1.5).
question.harnessCode:
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(0)
x=np.random.randn(64,256)*float(scale)
mu=x.mean(1,keepdims=True); var=x.var(1,keepdims=True)

question.explanation: Whatever the input scale, LN renormalizes each token to ~unit variance — that scale-invariance is the whole point.

slides.title: Pre-norm vs post-norm (why the field switched)
slides.body:
The original **Vaswani et al. (2017)** transformer placed LN *after* the residual add — **post-norm**: $\text{LN}(x+\text{Sublayer}(x))$. This configuration requires careful learning-rate warmup and becomes increasingly unstable as depth grows past roughly 12 layers, because the residual identity path is itself renormalized every layer, eroding the clean gradient highway.

**Pre-norm** — $x+\text{Sublayer}(\text{LN}(x))$ — normalizes only the sublayer's *input*, leaving the $x$ identity path untouched, so gradients flow through arbitrarily deep stacks without warmup.

The systematic study of this distinction was made rigorous by **Ruibin Xiong**, Yunchang Yang, Di He, Kai Zhao, Shuxin Zheng, Chen Xing, Huishuai Zhang, Yanyan Lan, Liwei Wang, and **Tie-Yan Liu** in *"On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture"* (ICML 2020), who proved theoretically why pre-norm stabilizes training. Essentially all modern deep transformers — **GPT-3** (96 layers), **LLaMA** (32–80 layers), **Mistral**, **Falcon** — use pre-norm. This single placement choice is what makes those depths trainable and ties directly to the residual lesson next.

slides.title: RMSNorm — the current default
slides.body:
**RMSNorm** was introduced by **Biao Zhang** and **Rico Sennrich** in *"Root Mean Square Layer Normalization"* (NeurIPS 2019). The key insight: drop the mean-centering and the $\beta$ shift entirely, normalize only by the root-mean-square: $\text{RMSNorm}(x)=\gamma\odot x/\sqrt{\overline{x^2}+\epsilon}$, where $\overline{x^2}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_i x_i^2$.

Fewer arithmetic operations, fewer parameters (no $\beta$, no mean subtraction), and empirically no measured quality loss compared to full LayerNorm. The interpretation: the re-centering step that LayerNorm performs is not load-bearing for training stability — only the re-scaling is. RMSNorm is the default in **LLaMA** (Touvron et al., Meta 2023), **LLaMA-2**, **Mistral**, **Falcon**, **Gemma**, and most subsequent open-weight models. It is a clean example of ablating a mechanism down to the essential part once you understand what each component is actually doing.

question.question: Why did large models migrate from post-norm to pre-norm?
options: Pre-norm leaves the residual stream un-normalized, preserving the identity path so very deep stacks train stably
Post-norm cannot represent the same functions
Pre-norm removes the need for residual connections
question.explanation: Pre-norm normalizes only the *input* to each sublayer; the residual stream flows through unnormalized, keeping a clean gradient highway across depth. Post-norm renormalizes the stream every layer, which causes instability as depth grows — fatal for 50–100 layer models.

question.question: Diagnose the training instability.
question.scenario: Moving LayerNorm from pre-norm (inside the residual branch) to post-norm (after the residual add), a deep model now diverges early unless you add careful LR warmup.

rubricCriteria.description: post-norm normalizes x+F(x), so the identity/residual gradient path is renormalized every layer
that degrades the clean gradient highway with depth → early divergence without warmup
pre-norm normalizes only F's input, leaving the identity path intact → stable deep training (modern default)

question.explanation: Norm placement relative to the residual add decides whether the identity gradient path stays clean. Pre-norm keeps it clean; post-norm doesn't.

hints: Where is LN relative to the x + F(x) add?
Which placement leaves the identity path un-normalized?
slides.workedSolution: Pre-norm normalizes only F's input, so the residual identity path carries gradient undiminished through many layers — deep training is stable without warmup. Post-norm normalizes the sum, eroding that path.

question.question: Why do modern deep transformers prefer pre-norm (LN inside the residual branch)?
options: It preserves a clean identity gradient path, so very deep models train stably without heavy warmup
Pre-norm removes the need for residuals
question.explanation: Pre-norm: out = x + F(LN(x)) — the x path is never renormalized, so its gradient stays ~1 through depth. Post-norm renormalizes x+F(x) each layer.

slides.title: What to carry forward
slides.body: LayerNorm (Ba, Kiros, Hinton 2016) = per-token, batch-independent re-standardization with learned $\gamma,\beta$. It solved the internal covariate shift problem (Ioffe and Szegedy 2015) for sequences and variable-length inputs where BatchNorm cannot work. Pre-norm placement (Xiong et al. 2020) and the RMSNorm simplification (Zhang and Sennrich 2019) are the modern defaults that make deep stacks — GPT-3 at 96 layers, LLaMA at 80 layers — stable and efficient. Its inseparable partner is the **residual connection** — next.
